problem: VLN agents on Room-to-Room (e.g., Speaker-Follower, RCM, Self-Monitoring) do much worse in unseen environments than in seen ones. Prior speaker-based back translation only adds synthetic instructions for new routes in the same 60 or so training houses, so it cannot add environment variability.
motivation: A practical navigation robot has to work in houses it has never seen. The authors show that the number of training environments, not the number of labeled routes, is the bottleneck. Adding data from more environments gives a steeper success-rate curve than adding the same amount of data from all training environments. Extrapolation also predicts that SR saturates around 52% even if all 190K training-environment routes were human-labeled.
key_idea: Create 'new' environments by applying one dropout mask, shared across all views and viewpoints of an environment (environmental dropout), to the visual features. Then run speaker back translation in these dropped-out environments, with the same mask tied between speaker and follower, to produce synthetic (environment, path, instruction) triplets for fine-tuning an IL+RL agent.
insight:
Augmentation must be consistent across views and viewpoints to act like a genuinely different environment. Ablations on R2R val-unseen SR (Table 2):
- IL+RL alone reaches 46.5.
- Back translation raises it to 48.2.
- Adding i.i.d. feature dropout gives 48.4, essentially no gain.
- Environmental dropout with untied speaker and follower masks gives 49.0.
- Environmental dropout with the mask tied between speaker and follower gives 52.2. This is +5.7 over IL+RL, about 3x the gain of plain back translation.

The same ordering holds with ground-truth semantic-view features, where dropout removes whole object classes: 49.5 → 50.5 (BT) → 50.2 (feat drop) → 52.0 (env drop). This supports the 'remove an object class' intuition. Back translation on the unlabeled target environments themselves gives 61.9, or 64.5 with env drop. This confirms that environment diversity, not instruction count, limits generalization. For the IL+RL mixture, the IL term regularizes RL: RL alone reaches only 24.0 SR, versus 43.6 for IL and 46.5 for the mixture.
method: Panoramic encoder-decoder follower: Bi-LSTM instruction encoder. Attentive LSTM decoder attends over 36 view features (ResNet-152 plus heading/elevation cos/sin) and then over instruction words. It scores navigable viewpoints by bilinear alignment with the instruction-aware hidden state h~_t, which (unlike Speaker-Follower) is also fed back as the LSTM's recurrent input.

IL+RL mixture (stage 1): behavioral cloning (teacher-forced shortest-path actions) and A2C with sampled actions share weights and roll out two independent routes. Loss is L_RL + λ_IL·L_IL. Reward is +3/−3 for stopping within/outside 3 m, plus shaped reward d_{t-1}−d_t per step; γ=0.9.

Enhanced speaker (backward model): two stacked Bi-LSTMs. A route encoder over ground-truth action features attends to the 36 surrounding views, a context encoder reads the attended features, and an attentive LSTM decoder generates the instruction. Reported gain is about +3 BLEU-4 over Speaker-Follower's speaker.

Back translation (stage 2): sample unlabeled shortest-path routes (about 190K exist in the training environments; R2R labels about 7%). The speaker generates instructions for them, and the agent is fine-tuned with IL+RL on the synthetic triplets. Half of each batch uses the supervised loss and half the semi-supervised loss.

Environmental dropout: one Bernoulli mask ξ^E (rate 0.4, scaled by 1/(1−p)) is applied to the 2048-d ResNet feature of every view at every viewpoint of an environment, leaving orientation features untouched. This mimics removing a consistent visual 'object class' and keeps the connectivity graph. The mask is resampled each iteration, shared across environments in a batch for stability, and tied between speaker and follower.

Test-time variants: beam search with state-factored Dijkstra (as in Speaker-Follower). Pre-exploration applies back translation with env dropout on the unlabeled test/val-unseen environments before single-run navigation.

setting.backbone: ResNet-152 (ImageNet-pretrained, frozen features) + Bi-LSTM encoder / attentive LSTM decoder follower and LSTM speaker (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: R2R train (61 envs, 14,025 instructions), plus speaker-generated instructions for unlabeled shortest-path routes in the training environments (out of ~190K possible routes), with environmental-dropout features. The pre-explore variant additionally back-translates on the unlabeled evaluation (unseen) environments.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 discretized views as ResNet-152 features + heading/elevation)
setting.privileged: none for single run. Beam-search variant explores many routes before choosing one. Pre-explore variant accesses the test environments (unlabeled routes/images) for back-translation fine-tuning.

results:
On the R2R test-unseen leaderboard the agent ranked #1 in all three setups:
- Single run: 51.5 SR / 0.47 SPL, beating Self-Monitoring (48.0 SR) and RCM (0.38 SPL).
- Beam search: 68.9 SR, versus RCM's 63.0.
- Pre-exploration: 63.9 SR / 0.61 SPL, versus RCM's 60.5 / 0.59.

On val-unseen, the full single-run model reaches 52.2 SR / 0.48 SPL. That is +5.7 SR over the IL+RL baseline (46.5) and +4.0 over plain back translation (48.2).
limitations: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning use val-unseen SR (early stopping), so val-unseen numbers are optimistic.

Environmental dropout acts on frozen ResNet feature dimensions, not real objects. It is a heuristic proxy for new environments, and the connectivity graph and layout of the training houses are unchanged. The pre-explore variant needs access to the test environments.
Evaluated only on R2R with discrete nav-graph actions and panoramic features. Beam search yields impractically long trajectories (SPL ≈ 0.01).
